idiom_name: Moq Mock<IPriceService> with strict behaviour, injected as the interface
implementation_notes: Interfaces plus Moq cover the object seam: Mock<IPriceService> with MockBehavior.Strict fails on unexpected calls, Setup states canned answers through expression trees, and the mock object is injected as IPriceService so the client cannot tell it apart from the real client. When the service is spoken to over HTTP the cheaper seam is the transport: derive from HttpMessageHandler, override SendAsync, and build the HttpClient over it, which also exercises the real serializer and status handling. Hand-written fakes remain the clear choice when the stand-in needs deterministic behaviour rather than recorded interactions, and generated gRPC clients cover the production seam.
pitfalls: A handler derived from HttpMessageHandler may be called concurrently by the HttpClient, so its state has to be thread-safe - the API documentation states this requirement explicitly.
Loose mocks answer every call with a default, so unconfigured operations quietly return null tasks or zero values and the error path never runs; use MockBehavior.Strict wherever possible.
A mocked interface drifts from a remote contract you do not own, so keep the vendor type behind an internal interface instead of mocking the vendor's surface directly.

variants.name: Fake HttpMessageHandler under the real HttpClient
variants.idiom_name: class StubHandler : HttpMessageHandler with an overridden SendAsync
variants.implementation_notes: Substituting the transport instead of the interface keeps the production client, its serialization and its status handling intact and turns a remote service into a local function from HttpRequestMessage to HttpResponseMessage. Reach for it when the request shape or the failure handling is what the test must prove; keep the handler thread-safe and dispose the HttpClient it is attached to.
pitfalls: The handler must be reusable across concurrent calls, because HttpClient does not serialize its handler invocations.
Stubbing the handler hides base-address, header and retry configuration; assert the request the client really produced rather than only the response it consumed.

variants.name: Hand-written deterministic fake implementing the interface
variants.idiom_name: class FakePriceService : IPriceService with canned data
variants.implementation_notes: A small class implementing the interface with an in-memory dictionary is the cheapest stand-in and the most readable: no library, no expression trees, and it can carry real behaviour (validation, invariants) rather than only recorded answers. It is also the only form worth reusing outside tests, for example as an offline mode.
pitfalls: A fake that never fails cannot test failure handling: keep the throw path reachable and covered.
Because it implements the interface by hand, a contract change breaks it only at compile time - which is the point, so keep the annotation to the interface and avoid dynamic or object-typed access.
